text:
Both premises are shaky, so I'd drop the Einstein story. He didn't fail math. He was top of his class in it and had mastered calculus by about 15. The myth likely comes from a misread grading scale (Swiss schools flipped their scale) and his failing the non-science sections of a university entrance exam at 16. A kid who checks this, and many do, will then discount the rest of your message.

"Grades don't matter" is also too strong. They affect course placement, scholarships, and admissions, and they're a feedback signal about what's been learned. A kid who later finds that out may stop trusting your advice.

A more accurate and more useful message: grades measure one narrow thing, how well you did on specific tasks at a specific time. They don't measure your worth, your intelligence, or your ceiling. A bad grade is information about what to fix, not a verdict. Effort and learning matter more than the number, and the number still has real consequences.

If you want true stories of late bloomers or setbacks, there are better ones: Thomas Edison's teachers reportedly clashed with him and he left school early (though the "told he was too stupid to learn" version is embellished), and Michael Jordan's cut from his varsity team is well documented, though he was a sophomore placed on JV rather than flatly rejected. Use them as examples of resilience, not proof that school performance is irrelevant.

If your kid is stressed about a particular grade, the framing that helps most is usually "what happened, and what would you do differently?" rather than reassurance that it doesn't matter.
